Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Ravi sat in the quiet of his accountant’s cubicle, fingers frozen over the keyboard, the sudden clatter of a coffee mug hitting the breakroom counter sending a jolt through his chest. His heart hammered, his palms damp, and for a moment the fluorescent lights seemed to dim—not because they actually did, but because his mind had dropped him somewhere else, somewhere he could not put into words. He was thirty-six years old, divorced, living alone in a suburban apartment that felt more like a bunker than a home. He had come to therapy at his boss’s insistence after that morning’s incident—a colleague shouting across the floor had triggered something so visceral that Ravi had ended up in the bathroom, hands braced against the sink, gasping for air. He could not explain what had happened. He could not explain any of it.

The event that had shaped him happened when he was eight. He had been sitting at the top of the stairs in his family’s house in New Jersey, listening to his father’s voice rise and then the sharp crack of a hand against flesh, his mother’s cry. He had frozen, unable to move, unable to call out. The memory never came back as a story he could tell; it came as a picture—the pattern on the stair runner, the smell of curry and sweat, the thud of a body hitting a wall—and with it the same terror, undimmed by decades. He could not find words for it. When his therapist asked what he remembered, Ravi shook his head and said, “I just see it. I feel it.” That was all.

In the years that followed, Ravi learned to keep watch. At work, he chose a desk with his back to the wall, his eyes scanning the corridor every time someone passed. He flinched at raised voices in meetings and felt his body lock into a protective tension that never fully released. He was constantly aware of exits, of sudden movements, of the pitch of a conversation shifting toward anger. His colleagues thought he was just intense, maybe anxious. They did not know that every small reminder—the slam of a door, the scrape of a chair, a man’s voice booming in laughter—could instantaneously, without warning, drop him back onto those stairs. He could not talk about any of it. The words felt stuck.

His marriage had ended two years ago. His wife had described him as emotionally unreachable, always on guard, never able to relax. Ravi had not argued. He knew she was right, but he also knew that his body did not give him a choice. He had come to believe that bad things simply happened, and that he could do nothing to stop them—not then, not now. That helplessness had seeped into everything: his job, his relationships, his sense of himself. He used to be a happy person, he remembered that dimly; now misery felt like his baseline, a gray wash over every day. And what gnawed at him most was the injustice—the fact that his father had faced no consequences, had never been held accountable. That thought simmered constantly, an ember of anger that he could not put out.

Avoidance had become a quiet habit. He stopped attending family gatherings where his father might appear. He changed the subject whenever conversations turned to childhood. He avoided any movie or show with domestic conflict. The consequence was a narrowing life—fewer friends, longer silences, a growing dread that he was failing at being human. His divorce had been the first major loss; now his job performance was slipping. He could not concentrate, could not sit still, was always scanning, always bracing.

What finally brought Ravi to the office of a clinical psychologist was that morning’s attack: the shout from across the floor, the rush of adrenaline, the complete loss of control. His boss had pulled him aside, concerned, and offered the company’s employee assistance program. Ravi had taken the card numbly. Now, sitting in the therapist’s chair, he was afraid—afraid that he would never feel safe, that the happiness he once knew was gone for good, that he would always be this coiled, watchful person. But he was also, beneath that fear, searching for something: a way to stop the triggers from hijacking him, to make sense of the wordless terror, to believe, just once, that the next bad thing did not have to happen.
